newsitem.title: USA: COMEX copper ends down, but further gains seen.
newsitem.headline: COMEX copper ends down, but further gains seen.

text.p: COMEX copper ended weaker but still sharply up on the week as LME stocks continue to fall amid production problems and strikes, indicating further gains in the cards, dealers said.
The market was sold off Friday because it had become overbought technically and was due for a correction, John Gross of the Copper Journal said.
"We could pull back a little bit further, but overall, the uptrend is still very much in place," Gross said.
By close of trade Friday, the 9 and 14 day RSI were down to 65 percent compared with over 70 percent - seen as overbought territory - earlier in the week.

Dealers noted that COMEX stocks continued to rise and the traditionally slow seasonal summer period approached. Not all the stock hike could be attributed to arbitrage-related shipments from LME warehouses, and could also be indicative of the surge in copper imports into the U.S. while exports have fallen, analysts said.
LME stocks Friday fell 1,675 tonnes to 125,650 tonnes.
COMEX stocks Friday rose 678 short tons to 46,642 tons.
Most-active July COMEX settled 0.75 cent weaker at 120.60 cents. Spot June went out 0.85 cent lower at 120.25 cents.
In Chile heavy rains briefly stopped work at Phelps Dodge's Candelaria mine Thursday but no production was lost, company officials said Friday.
The strike at Inco in Canada, which began June 2, continued this week, will deprive the market of 9,000 tonnes a month of copper if it lasts, an analyst said.
The Ok Tedi copper mine in Papua New Guinea was still in the middle of a drought Friday and unable to ship concentrates, but the company insisted there would be no declaration of force majeure soon.
One Ok Tedi customer, LG Metals in South Korea, said a 10,000 tonne concentrate delivery had been delayed, but LG said it did not anticipate problems with feeding its smelter.

Despite Friday's correction, July still ended the week 3.45 cents firmer and some 20 cents above the close on June 14, 1996, the day following Sumitomo Corp's announcement of huge losses from copper dealings.
